name: Cris Kocian
title: Experimental Constraints on the Origin of ^{13}C-Depleted Martian Sediments in Gale Crater
authors: Cris Kocian^{1}, Christopher House^{1}, Jennifer Stern^{2}, Steven M. Bates^{2}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Greenbelt, MD, USA
abstract: In Gale Crater, the Curiosity rover foundorganic molecules with a wide range of carbon isotopic compositions. Methane (CH_{4}) released during pyrolysis by the Sample Analysis at Mars (SAM) instrument exhibits δ^{13}C values in the range of –137 ± 8‰ to +22 ±10‰. Ten of the twenty-four samples in this dataset are strongly depleted in ^{13}C(δ^{13}C < –70‰). Two hypotheses to explain this ^{13} Cdepletion with abiotic processes are 1) contamination of the derivatizing agentN-tert-butyldimethylsilyl-N-methyltrifluoroacetamide (MTBSTFA) and 2) photochemical deposition of formaldehyde (HCHO). MTBSTFA, which is present inthe background of the SAM instrument, has a δ^{13}C value of about –35‰and would produce CH_{4} if pyrolyzed. Alternatively, ultravioletradiation in the Martian atmosphere photolyzes carbon dioxide (CO_{2}) into carbon monoxide (CO) depleted in ^{13}C with a δ^{13}C ofapproximately –150‰. If this ^{13}C-depleted CO is furtherphotochemically reduced to HCHO it could deposit onto the surface and bedetected by Curiosity.\nTo test these hypotheses, we simulated SAMpyrolysis conditions in the laboratory and measured CH_{4} productionand carbon isotope fractionation from candidate compounds. Tetrakis (trimethylsilyl) silane (TKS) was used as an analog for MTBSTFA. Pyrolysis of TKS at low (75℃) and high (455℃) temperature cuts produced CH_{4}with δ^{13}C values from –49‰ to –43‰, which are not depleted enough toaccount for lower SAM measurements. In contrast, pyrolysis of HCHO at the sametemperature cuts produced primarily CO and minimal CH_{4}. Despitelower CH_{4} yields, HCHO derived from ^{13}C-depletedatmospheric CO could reproduce the SAM δ^{13}C values if the isotopiccomposition of photolyzed CO is retained. These results support photochemicallyproduced HCHO as a more likely abiotic source of the ^{13}C-depleted CH_{4}detected by Curiosity than MTBSTFA contamination.

name: Liz Tofte
title: Quantifying Seasonal Sea Ice Melt and Sediment Plume Development at Arctic River Mouths
authors: Liz Tofte^{1}, Anastasia Piliouras^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: The Arctic is warming at more than four timesthe global average. This warming has led to significant changes in Arctic riverhydrology, including increased discharge, greater sediment supply, and earlierspring freshet onset. These upstream changes affect the coastal zone – dynamicland–ocean interfaces where seasonal riverine and oceanic processes regulateprimary productivity – making them particularly vulnerable to climate change. Coastal sea ice melt and sediment plume development are two seasonal processesthat directly respond to freshwater, heat, and sediment export from rivers, yetthey remain under-observed. Quantifyinghow these processes behave and change over time can provide insight into howthe coastal zone is responding to changing hydrology.\nThis study investigates six major Arctic rivermouths: the Yukon, Colville, and Mackenzie in North America, and theOb-Yenisei, Kolyma, and Lena in Eurasia. The objectives are to (1) characterizetypical seasonal patterns of coastal sea ice melt and sediment plumedevelopment, (2) assess changes over two decades, and (3) compare variabilitybetween systems. Sea ice and plume behaviors were analyzed using MODIS-derivedsea ice products and MODIS imagery, respectively.\nResults show that river mouths follow twoprimary ice melt regimes: initiating directly at the shoreline *{or} atoffshore flaw leads, suggesting differences in dominant processes drivingcoastal ice melt initiation. As temperatures continue to increase into thesummer, sediment plumes develop, with turbidity peaking in early summerfollowing snowmelt and occasionally in late summer due to storm-drivenresuspension. Eurasian rivers show significant trends in sea ice behavior, including a shortening melt season at the Lena and Ob–Yenisei and earlierlandfast melt at the Kolyma. Across all systems, sediment delivery to the coastis occurring earlier, with significantly earlier plume onset at the Lena, Kolyma, and Mackenzie. Overall, Arctic coastal processes are shifting inresponse to rapid warming, though the magnitude and timing of change vary amongriver systems, reflecting strong local controls.

name: Renan Beckman
title: Exploring zircon dark zones throughcathodoluminescence and trace elements: New insights from the Ruby Star Granodiorite, Arizona
authors: Renan Beckman^{1}, Herve Rezeau^{2}, Erik Schoonover^{1}, Maureen Feineman^{1} , Jesse Reimink^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2} Earth Resources Laboratory, Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA
abstract: Copperis critical to the global energy transition, and demand is rising rapidly. The main global copper sources are Porphyry Copper Deposits (PCDs). New PCDs are becoming more challenging to find, and major discoveries from thepast decade are being found deeper in the subsurface. To improve explorationstrategies, a holistic understanding of the processes that drive PCDemplacement is required.\nRecent work has focused on accessory igneousminerals (e. g. zircon, apatite) within intrusions associated with PCDs asrecorders of magmatic and hydrothermal evolution. Zircon textural featuresrevealed by Cathodoluminescence (CL) record variations in the chemicalevolution through its characteristic oscillatory growth zoning. This studyspecifically focuses on zircon “dark” growth zones that are commonly observedin porphyry intrusions, yet poorly studied (e. g., Bajo de la Allumbrera; Buretet al., 2016). In Bajo de la Alumbrera, zircon dark zones display anomalously high concentrations of uraniumand rare earth elements (REE), and are interpreted as relics of a maficrecharge event (Buret et al., 2016).\nTo test petrogenetic models for zircon darkzone growth, and their possible usefulness as a geochemical vector for PCDs, zircon grains from the Ruby Star Granodiorite associated with world-classsierrita PCD were depth profiled via Laser Ablation Split Stream Inductively Coupled Mass Spectrometer (LASS-ICP-MS). Zircons from the Ruby Star Granodiorite commonly exhibit dark growth zones characterized by enriched U, Th, and REEs. After rotating these grains 90º and polishing to expose the depthprofile, we use SEM imaging and electron microprobe analyses to evaluate themorphology and chemistry of zircon grains. Here we present these findings anddiscuss their implications for the petrogenetic mechanisms that form zircondark zones in intrusions associated with PCDs, and evaluate their potential tobetter understand emplacement and as a geochemical indicator to identify“fertile” intrusions.

name: Lillian Miller
title: Using InSAR, SAR Offset Tracking, and GNSSto Investigate the August 28, 2020 Bedrock Landslide Within the Irazú-Turrialba Volcanic Complex, Costa Rica
authors: Lillian Miller^{1}, Dr. Christelle Wauthier^{1}, Young Cheol Kim^{1}, Cyril Muller^{2}, Esteban Chaves^{2}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2} Observatorio Vulcanológico y Sismológico de Costa Rica (OVSICORI-UNA), Universidad Nacional, Costa Rica
abstract: The presence of landslides in volcanicsettings is a significant threat, as large landslides on volcanic edifices canlead to cascading hazards, including smaller landslides, debris avalanches, ormagma chamber depressurization. On August 28, 2020, the Volcanological and Seismological Observatory of Costa Rica (OVSICORI) observed a landslide in avalley adjacent to Irazú Volcano. The landslide occurred within the Irazú-Turrialba Volcanic Complex outside of San José, Costa Rica. Turrialba, the second volcano within the complex and just 10 km from Irazú, saw renewedactivity beginning in 2010 and continuing through 2022 and has sparked concernof potential reactivation of Irazú and associated hazards. The cause of thislandslide is currently unknown, but the renewed activity at Turrialba hintsthat the landslide may have been driven by underground magmatic activity withinthe volcanic complex. We propose to leverage optical and radar imagery intandem with Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) positional data toanswer: (1) was the August 28, 2020 landslide initiated by renewedmagmatic movement below the Irazú-Turrialba Volcanic Complex? And (2) was subsidence a precursor to the landslide? We hypothesize that thelandslide was not caused by renewed magmatic movement and that subsidence was aprecursor to the landslide. GNSS results show the landmass experienced 3.5m of accelerating subsidence over three years leading up to the landslide, with4 m of subsidence occurring during the landslide. However, Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) analysis of Sentinel-1 C-band SAR data reveals> 1 m of subsidence across the same period, likely due to high rates ofdeformation, fast temporal decorrelation, and vegetation within the volcaniccomplex. Continued work is being done to leverage offset tracking with Planetoptical data and high-resolution COSMO-Sky Med X-band SAR data to capture thedisplacement and more accurately match the GNSS displacement of the landmass.

name: Ethan Heidtman
title: Modeling and mitigation of riverinesaltwater intrusion hazards using reservoir operations: a case study in thetidal Susquehanna River
authors: Ethan Heidtman^{1} and Antonia Hadjimichael^{1, 2}
institutions: ^{1} Penn State University Department of Geosciences\n^{2} Penn State University Earth and Environmental Systems Institute
abstract: Multi-purpose reservoirs are criticalinfrastructure for the management of water resources, and reservoir operationsmust often balance multiple competing water demands. Climate change is animportant threat to the resiliency of water resources in these reservoirs, asit can limit the efficacy of historical operations strategies as well as waterdemands and availability. The Conowingo Reservoir, a large multi-purposereservoir located in Pennsylvania and Maryland along the Susquehanna River, hasbeen managed actively for decades, yet current operating policies fail toadequately account for internal system variability and emerging threats toregional water resource reliability. Havre de Grace, Maryland, a smallcommunity at the mouth of the Susquehanna River, sources drinking water fromthe river, and during periods of low riverine freshwater flow and certainweather conditions, saline waters from Chesapeake Bay can intrude upstream, degrading public water supply and corroding infrastructure.\nTo address this emerging problem, we firstdevelop a statistical model for saltwater intrusion at the Havre de Gracedrinking water intake using historical discharge, tide, and wind data from 2007– 2024. Salinity responses to wind and tidal forcing under low flow conditionsare rare and nonlinear, such as in October 2016, when drinking water exceededthe EPA Secondary Standard for Total Dissolved Solids for a 2-week period. These events highlight the need for targeted reservoir releases prior to and duringsalinity events, and results indicate that the model can identifyintrusion-prone conditions more than 10 days in advance. Future work willincorporate this forecast model into a simulation-optimization framework forthe Conowingo, training adaptive, state-aware, and dynamic release policiesthat release water from the reservoir downstream to flush out intrudingsaltwater while continuing to satisfy pre-existing regional water demands.

name: Arthur Lo
title: Analysis of Ground Deformation Precedingthe December 2020 – May 2021 Summit Eruption at Kīlauea Volcano, Hawai’i
authors: Arthur Wan Ki Lo^{1}, Christelle Wauthier^{1, 2}, Young Cheol Kim^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2} Institute for Computational and Data Sciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: The 2020 summit eruption at Kīlauea Volcano, Hawai’i marked a new phase of eruptive activity at Kīlauea’s summit followingthe end of the 2018 Lower East Rift Zone eruption. Seismicity and grounddeformation had been reported prior to the eruption, including an intrusionbeneath the summit caldera on 2 December 2020. To investigate the geometry andvolume of the 2 December intrusion, we processed interferograms using ascendingand descending orbit Sentinel-1 SAR data with acquisition dates spanning 2 December2020. To investigate long-term summit deformation prior to the eruption, wealso processed Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) time-series ofKīlauea using data from Sentinel-1 satellites (January to mid-December 2020).\nFor the interferograms, we measuredline-of-sight (LOS) displacements ranging from about 14 to -2.8 cm and 7 to-4.2 cm respectively for the ascending and descending orbit interferogram. Weinverted the LOS displacements and modelled the intrusion using analyticsolutions for point source, rectangular dislocation, penny-shaped crack andspheroid models in an elastic half space. The deformation coincides with thelocation of a linear feature within the summit caldera, which suggests thatdeformation observed in early December 2020 could be associated with movementalong a caldera fault.\nUsing the time-series, we found a steadyincrease in LOS displacement within the caldera. We separated the time-seriesinto 3 periods: P1 (January – early November), P2 (early November – early December), and P3 (early December – mid-December). We observed distinctdeformation patterns, including localized deformation within Halema’uma’uCrater during P1, a marked increase in displacement rates within the calderafor P2 and deformation likely associated with the intrusion in P3. The patternof the localized deformation during P1 coincides with the location of theeruptive vents which formed during the December 2020 eruption. This mayrepresent a pathway along which magma was transported for the eruption.

name: Dan Cove
title: Laboratory methods to constrain thehabitability of extreme environments
authors: Daniel Cove^{1}, Chris House^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Habitability, an environment’s ability tosupport life on some scale, is a concept that is pervasive in our discussionsof planets in outer space. Whether the focus is on distant exoplanets, neighboring worlds in our solar system, or the planet Earth itself at variouspoints in the past, physicochemical conditions which constitute habitabilityare constantly redefined and speculated upon. One characteristic shared by eachof these example locations is that they are not readily accessible *{in situ}, whether due to a spatial or temporal barrier. For observed or theorized environments in such places, the development of laboratory simulations isnecessary.\nThis study develops a series of laboratoryassays that can be subjected to simulations of exotic environments to constrainhabitability along a continuum from a single aqueous biological reaction tocomplete cell division. The assay representing the low end of the habitabilityspectrum is activity of the bioessential enzyme phosphatase, which cleavesphosphate ions from larger substrates to eventually create ATP for cellularenergy storage. Such enzyme activity can be observed and quantified in lab experimentsusing ^{31}P NMR spectroscopy and represents the minimum biologicalreaction for the host environment to be considered habitable. The higher end ofthe habitability spectrum is represented by the replication of a (likelyextremophilic) bacterial cell. The survival and replication of a bacterialculture subject to simulated conditions can be monitored using both fluorescentdye staining techniques coupled with microscopy and labelled isotopeincorporation coupled with Raman spectroscopy. Creating a reasonable labsimulation of exotic planetary conditions and using these habitability proxiesto work from one end of the continuum to the other will allow for betterunderstanding of habitability as we know it and help to clarify keyastrobiological target locations across the solar system and beyond for futurespace missions.

name: Mingxi Hu
title: The Paradox of Cyclonic Storms in a Cold Pennsylvanian Equatorial Region
authors: Mingxi Hu^{1}, Paul M. Myrow^{2}, and Michael P. Lamb^{3}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University\n^{2} Department of Geology, Colorado College\n^{3} Divisionof Geological and Planetary Sciences, California Institute of Technology
abstract: Earth has experienced extreme past climates, and the Pennsylvanian equatorial climate has been widely debated: whiletraditionally viewed as warm, recent studies controversially suggestedwidespread cold conditions and low-altitude glaciation. One tool that has notbeen widely evaluated is the state of the sea, which is powerful as the stateof the sea and ocean–atmospheric linkages are highly latitude dependent.\nWe conducted a paleohydraulic analysis onstorm-generated, hummocky bedforms preserved in marine intervals of the Fountain and Minturn Formations in Pangea’s paleoequator. Reconstructed waveperiods and fetch distances indicate the presence of large gravity waves formedunder gale-to-hurricane strength winds. These bedforms therefore requiredcyclonic storms driven by high Coriolis vorticity and high sea surfacetemperatures. These results are at odds with a cold equatorial hypothesis, andchallenge published paleolatitude estimates (<5 degree north) for the Colorado region, suggesting that Pennsylvanian tropical conditions werefundamentally different than previously posited.

name: Ava Spangler
title: Collaborative Development of a Pluvial Flood Model and Adaptation Strategies to Advance Resilience in Baltimore
authors: Ava Spangler^{1, 2}, Antonia Hadjimichael^{1, 2}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2} Earth and Environmental Systems Institute, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Climate change is intensifying the hydrologiccycle, leading to more frequent and severe rainfall-driven (pluvial) floodingin urban areas. In the mid-Atlantic US cities, aging and under-designedstormwater infrastructure is increasingly strained by these events, resultingin recurring damage to property and disruptions to transportation networks. Inthis study, we combine community engagement with hydrologic modeling to developand evaluate potential urban flood adaptation strategies. Over a three-year period, local technical experts and community representatives met regularly to discussflooding concerns, identify priorities, and co-develop adaptation strategies. These discussions informed the development of an urban flooding model (EPAStorm Water Management Model) for the Baltimore Harbor watershed, the focuslocation of this study. The flooding model integrates complex surface andsubsurface stormwater infrastructure data, local expert knowledge, andcommunity insights. We simulate stakeholder-prioritized adaptations, such asgreen and gray infrastructure strategies. Model results demonstrate thatenhanced infrastructure maintenance is the most effective adaptation forreducing flood depths, but has varied effects across the watershed, and canincrease flooding in some locations. Spatially concentrated greening provideslimited benefit to the watershed as a whole, but moderate benefit in communitypriority areas. Together, these adaptations have the potential to reduce flooddepths by as much as 58% in some locations, greatly reducing property damageand mobility impacts, primary concerns of stakeholders. Future work willimplement robust optimization tools to search for adaptations which meetstakeholder objectives and perform highly under varied future climateconditions. This work contributes to the expanding literature on collaborativemodeling and demonstrates that community-engaged approaches can enhance modelcredibility and generate more actionable insights for communities seeking tostrengthen climate resilience.

name: Bailey Hoplight
title: Elevated CO_{2 } Effects on Water Isotope Fractionation in Trees
authors: Bailey Hoplight^{1}, Max Lloyd^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, the Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Plant tissues and their oxygen isotope (δ^{18}O) compositions are considered valuable records of paleoenvironmental change, capturing shifts in key climate parameters such as temperature, water source, and water availability. Plant tissue δ^{18}O represents the combinedinfluence of these processes on the physiochemical response of the plant, andthis understanding has been leveraged to reconstruct temperature andhydroclimate conditions across the recent geologic timescale. However, it isimportant to understand how additional factors could confound this framework. One such factor that remains poorly constrained is the response of plant tissueδ^{18}O under varying atmospheric CO_{2} concentrations.\nThis study aims to investigate the effects ofelevated CO_{2} concentrations on the δ^{18}O isotopiccomposition of plant materials. *{Ginkgo biloba} trees were grown inchambers for six growing seasons with CO_{2} concentrations rangingfrom 425 to 1000 ppm. δ^{18}O compositions were measured from both bulkwood and cellulose of latewood across multiple annual growth rings. Ifresulting δ^{18}O values are found to be quantitatively related to CO_{2}concentrations, then previous and future paleoclimate reconstructions based onthe isotopic composition of plant tissues will require careful (re-) calibrationto atmospheric CO_{2}.\nThis presentation will highlight preliminaryresults, emerging isotopic trends, and offer initial interpretations as to howthese patterns relate to physiological responses of plants under elevated CO_{2}conditions.

name: Mila Matney
title: Orbitrap-MS Characterization of Polycyclic Aromatic Hydrocarbons on the Asteroid Bennu
authors: Mila Matney^{1}, Kate Freeman^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: The return of material from the carbonaceouschondrite asteroid Bennu by the OSIRIS-REx mission provides a uniqueopportunity to explore pristine organic matter sourced from the origins of the Solar System. Many classes of organic compounds have been identified on Bennu, including bio-relevant molecules like amino acids, nucleobases, and sugars. Aromatic compounds found in carbonaceous chondrites are of particular interestas they are prevalent both in soluble and insoluble organic fractions and havediverse potential origins, ranging from cold interstellar chemistries to hightemperature reactions in circumstellar environments in addition to reactionsoccurring post-accretion on the asteroid parent body. Previous analyses haveconfirmed the presence of 2-6 ring polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) on Bennu, with a greater proportion of smaller forms than in studied meteorites. We will further investigate these trends using Orbitrap mass spectrometry (MS) which combines high mass resolution and low detection limits to allow foraccurate measurements in sample-limited situations, like that of Bennu. Thequantification of major PAH species and overall population of aromatics will bereported on, in the context of other meteorite samples and the history of the Solar System.

name: Alejo Giraldo
title: Three new Atherospermataceae species fromthe middle Eocene add 35 million years to the family’s Australian history
authors: L. Alejandro Giraldo^{1}, Peter Wilf^{1}, Raymond J. Carpenter^{2 }
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2} School of Biological Sciences, Adelaide University, Adelaide, SA, Australia
abstract: The southern sassafrases (Atherospermataceae) are a small plant family of ca. 16 species, ten of which are endemic to Australia. Despite being a dominant element of Australian rainforests today, the earliest continental record of the family dates to the Plio–Pleistocene of Tasmania, thereby limiting interpretations of Atherospermataceae biogeography. Here, we describe three new Atherospermataceae species based on organicallypreserved leaves from the middle Eocene (ca. 41–38 Ma) Anglesea flora of southeastern Australia, representing the terminal phase of Gondwana. The fossils wereexamined using light, epifluorescence, and confocal microscopy, and comparedwith extant material, including all extant Atherospermataceae genera, using theliterature, herbarium specimens, cleared-leaf material, and cuticlepreparations. Based on leaf architecture and cuticular morphology, two speciesare assigned to the living genera *{Doryphora} and *{Laurelia}, while athird, characterized by a densely papillate abaxial epidermis not seen in anyliving member of the family, is placed in a new fossil genus. These fossilsextend the Australian macrofossil record of Atherospermataceae by ca. 35million years, provide the only pre-Neogene evidence of the family in Australia, and show that Atherospermataceae were already diverse andwell-established in southeastern Australia by the middle Eocene, during thefinal stage of Gondwanan fragmentation. The occurrence of *{Laurelia} at Anglesea provides direct evidence that the genus, now extant in New Zealand andsouthern South America, once extended across a broader range than its modernrelicts and prior fossils indicate, and suggests that Australia could haveacted as the source or “stepping-stone” region for *{Laurelia} in New Zealand.

name: Mingxi Hu
title: Decoding the Late Paleozoic Ice Age Paradox: Basin-Scale Filtering of Global Climate Signals
authors: Mingxi Hu^{1}, Elizabeth Hajek^{1}, Brian Kelley^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: The stratigraphic record is our primaryarchive for understanding Earth’s climate history and dynamics, yet sedimentarybasins are active filters that "shred, " amplify, or distort originalclimate signals. This challenge is particularly acute in icehouse periods, suchas the Late Paleozoic Ice Age (LPIA), regarding its tropical hydroclimate, temperature, and atmospheric circulations. It remains unclear whether thesecontradictions reflect fundamentally different mechanisms to the Pleistocene, orour inability to read LPIA records across boundary conditions.\nI propose to resolve this ambiguity bysystematically comparing two equatorial Laurentia basins: the Bird Springs (BS) passive margin and the Midcontinent epeiric sea (MS). While both experiencedsimilar tropical climate, they differed in oceanography, terrestrial flux, andaccommodation. By integrating lithostratigraphy, geochemistry (B/Ga forpaleosalinity; CIA for weathering), and fauna assemblages, I aim to quantifyhow basin boundary conditions tuned climate records. I hypothesize that therestricted MS basin amplifies high-frequency, regional "noises "decoupled from global trends, whereas the open-marine BS basin provides abetter-fidelity archive for global climate forcing. Further comparison to otherLPIA records from various latitudes and locations will test whether LPIAclimate patterns (e. g., ITCZ shifts) align with Pleistocene mechanisms. Thisresearch establishes sensitivity baselines for comparing local vs. globalsedimentary records, providing a critical framework for 1) reconstructing pastclimate, 2) predicting future climate with geographical differences, and 3) informing resource management.

name: Sabrina Ashik
title: Leakiness Variability in Arctic River Deltas from SWOT Water Surface Elevation Observations
authors: Sabrina Ashik^{1}, Anastasia Piliouras^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Arctic river deltas play a critical role inregulating the delivery of freshwater, sediment, and nutrients to the coastalocean, influencing sea ice dynamics and coastal ecosystems. Discharge andsediment concentrations are often measured upstream at the delta apex, and howthese fluxes are partitioned and redistributed across distributary networksremains poorly understood. Flow partitioning within these networks depends ontheir hydraulic structure, including the degree of lateral exchange between channelsand adjacent islands. One metric used to quantify this behavior ischannel-island “leakiness, ” formulated by Hines and Piliouras (2024), whichrepresents the likelihood of water leaving the channel as a function of channelgeometry and water surface gradient. Leakiness has been calculated for the Mackenzie Delta using historical water level and discharge data from gaugestations; however, its variability across Arctic systems remains poorlyconstrained at basin scales due to sparse in situ observations. In this study, we quantify temporal and spatial variability in channel-network leakinessacross major Arctic deltas using remotely sensed Water Surface Elevation (WSE) data from the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) mission.\nWe extracted SWOT WSE time series at apex andoutlet locations from August 2023 to January 2026, used WSE as a proxy forwater level, and calculated monthly leakiness values. We then evaluated therelationship between leakiness and discharge using the framework proposed by Hines and Piliouras (2024). Preliminary results indicate a consistent positiverelationship between discharge and leakiness at both apexes and outlets, withstronger sensitivity at the apex locations than at the outlets. However, we observeda large inter-delta difference, suggesting that leakiness-dischargerelationships derived from a single system cannot be generalized across Arcticdeltas. These findings advance our understanding of flow partitioning in Arcticdistributary networks and establish a foundation for quantifying large-scalehydraulic connectivity from satellite observations.

name: Ash Keenan
title: Morphodynamic Variability Between River Delta Experiments With Identical Input and Boundary Conditions
authors: Ash Keenan^{1}, Anastasia Piliouras^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, the Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Flume experiments are valuable tools forsimulating and studying complex sediment transport and morphodynamic processesthat are difficult to observe in natural environments. However, theseexperiments are resource-intensive and thus rarely repeated, raising questionsabout the reproducibility of results. This research utilizes a series of fiveidentical experiments (Su1–Su5) repeated under the same input and boundaryconditions in order to investigate the inherent variability between physicaldelta experiments. We examine variations in delta characteristics such as areagrowth, wetted frequency, perimeter/area ratio, shoreline roughness, andfractal dimension using overhead photography and 3D photogrammetry. Preliminaryresults show that area growth rates remain positive and approximately linearacross all trials, reflecting constant progradation under uniform water andsediment input, though final delta sizes diverge slightly. Wetted fractionvalues are comparable among experiments (means ~0.40–0.55), indicatingoccupation of a similar partially channelized regime. Perimeter/area ratioexhibits a consistent downward trend as deltas expand, with small fluctuationsdriven by planform differences. In contrast, shoreline roughness revealsmeaningful divergence: Su3 experienced a major late-stage channel avulsion thatproduced fewer, larger distributaries and a sustained increase in shorelinecomplexity relative to the other experiments, which were characterized bygradual channel migration and numerous smaller outlets. Fractal dimensioncaptures greater similarity of the shoreline overall but also reflects elevatedcomplexity in Experiment 3 following avulsion. Ongoing work will incorporateearlier experimental hours and analyze photogrammetry-derived digital elevationmodels to assess differences in slope and channel relief. Together, theseresults demonstrate that while many bulk morphodynamic metrics arestatistically similar under identical forcing, stochastic events can generatemeasurable divergence, underscoring the importance of replication inexperimental geomorphology.

name: Laura Kelsall
title: Microtextural controls on the dissolutionof monazite and zircon during biotite-dehydration melting
authors: Laura Kelsall^{1}, Peter Kelemen^{2}, Andrew Smye^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2} Columbia University, Lamont Doherty Earth Observatory, Palisades, NY, USA
abstract: Differentiation of the continental crust intoan upper layer enriched in heat-producing elements (U, Th, K) and acomplementary lower crust depleted in these elements is key for continentalstability (e. g., Mareschal & Jaupart, 2013; Sandiford et al., 2002). Recentanalysis indicates that ultrahigh temperatures (>900°C) may be required toeffectively redistribute U and Th from the lower to upper crust (Smye &Kelemen 2025). Such temperature requirements are at odds with equilibriumthermodynamic modelling (Yakymchuck & Brown, 2014), and so the exactmechanism that accounts for this observation is uncertain.\nHere we test the hypothesis that mineralarmouring modulates the dissolution of monazite and zircon—key Th and U carrierphases, respectively—in silicate melt produced during biotite-dehydrationmelting. We present microtextural and trace element geochemical observationsfrom a suite of aluminous metasedimentary rocks (Ivrea-Verbano Zone) thatpreserve a record of partial melting under peak temperatures spanning thebiotite-dehydration melting interval (700-900°C). Automated SEM mapping of thinsections reveals a strong positive correlation between biotite and monazitemodal abundances. In the amphibolite-facies samples 8-27% of monazite is eitherincluded or adjacent to biotite grains whereas in granulite-facies andultrahigh temperature samples that decreases to 0-22% and 0% respectively. Theamount of monazite included in garnet increases from 3-10% in amphibolite to75% in ultrahigh temperature samples. Zircon abundance is poorly correlated tobiotite but still shows a similar trend of decreasing association with biotite (15-44% to 0%) and increasing association with garnet (3-29% to 38%) fromamphibolite to ultrahigh temperature samples.\nThese findings suggest that the texturalavailability of accessory phases imposes an important control on the flux of Uand Th into silicate melt produced during anatexis. Prior to the consumption ofbiotite, included carrier phases may be shielded from interacting with melt; peritectic growth of garnet serves to sequester carrier phases in the residuum. Work is ongoing to incorporate this microtextural framework into a forwardmodel describing the evolution of melt U, Th concentrations during biotite-dehydrationmelting and to explore implications for crustal differentiation.

name: Drew Moreland
title: Understandinghow flow variability and sea level rise impact delta morphodynamics
authors: Andrew Moreland^{1 }, Liz Hajek^{1}, Anastasia Piliouras^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park PA, USA
abstract:
Global temperatures are rising, accelerating sea-level risethat threatens the stability of deltaic environments. More than 300 millionpeople live in or near vulnerable delta systems, many of which alreadyexperience land loss, subsidence, and amplified flood hazards. Global warmingis also influencing river discharge patterns, which can trigger more abruptavulsions and potentially deadly floods.
Most existing studies have examined sea-level rise and flowvariability independently. However, these processes often operatesimultaneously in deltas, meaning their combined effects on channel mobility, sediment distribution, and avulsion behavior remain poorly constrained. Thisproject aims to address this gap by experimentally investigating how sea levelrise and discharge variability affect delta dynamics both individually andtogether.
My experiments will be conducted in the Sediment and Natural Dynamics Basin for Observation and eXperiments (SANDBOX), a controlledphysical basin that allows direct manipulation of sea-level rise and dischargevariability. Over the course of my M. S. research, I will conduct approximatelynine experiments looking at how sea level rise and discharge variability willaffect channel mobility. Stratigraphic analyses will follow to quantifydifferences in sediment deposition and avulsion signatures across runs.
My hypothesis is that rising sea levelsand increased flow variability will accelerate shoreline change and increaseavulsion frequency in deltaic systems. From this we will learn more aboutstratigraphic stacking patterns and have a better understanding ofaccommodation and sediment supply. By linking sea-level forcing with flowvariability, it fills a key gap in geomorphology for interpreting naturaldeltas. The broader significance lies in improving hazard assessment andmanagement strategies for vulnerable coastal regions.

name: Doni Anderson
title: Exploring Deltaic Stratigraphy in Arctic Environments
authors: Doni Anderson^{1}, Anastasia Piliouras^{1}, Benjamin Cardenas^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: River deltas leave deposits that hold a usefulrecord of past environmental conditions. Arctic deltas on Earth provideinsights about how ice cover and permafrost affects depositional patterns, potentially holding clues to constrain identification of ancient deltas thatmay have formed under the influence of ice. Despite its current presence andabundance, deltaic stratigraphy in Arctic environments has not been heavilyexplored, limiting our understanding of ancient deltas. We aim to fill thisgap.\nWe used numerical models of deltamorphodynamics in Arctic conditions to examine how permafrost and ice impactdelta stratigraphy. We used stratal volumes produced by these models to exploredifferences between permafrost at varying erodibilities and different icethicknesses (no permafrost to 65% permafrost erodibility and no ice to 4.5m icethickness), and to quantify sand fraction throughout the delta. Preliminaryresults show that ice and permafrost have a noticeable impact on deltaformation. As ice thickness increases and permafrost erodibility decreases, there is an increase in mud in the delta plain, likely resulting from sandbeing bypassed out of the subaerial system because the permafrost inhibitsaccommodation for the sediment supply. Sand fraction generally decreases downdelta, but the combination of thicker ice and lower permafrost erodibilityresults in a shallower decrease in sand fraction in comparison with thinnerice/higher permafrost erodibility or no ice/no permafrost model run outputs. Whenice thickness decreases and permafrost erodibility increases, there is moremixing of the mud and sand sediment throughout the delta, resulting in a highersand fraction overall. Future analyses will describe channel patterns byquantifying channel lateral mobility and vertical stacking and measuringchannel geometry. This work will continue to explore the implications of thesefindings for connections between ancient delta stratigraphy and paleoclimate. These first steps could prove useful for ancient delta studies on places suchas Mars where its paleoclimate is still uncertain.

name: Edo Nurshal
title: Fault Slip and Fluid Flow: Seismic Source Analysis of Slip Patches and Their Role in Fault Permeability
authors: M. Edo Nurshal^{1}, Junpeng Wang^{2}, Pengliang Yu^{1, 2}, Tushar Mittal^{1}, Derek Elsworth^{1, 2}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2} Department of Energy and Mineral Engineering, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Fluid injections can trigger faultreactivation, microearthquakes (MEQs), and permeability changes that arecritical for geothermal energy production and subsurface waste disposal. Recentstudies have shown that fault permeability can be quantitatively predicted fromthe cumulative seismic moment released by MEQs. To investigate the physicalmechanisms behind this relationship, we conducted laboratory fault reactivationexperiments on a Utah FORGE granitoid sample and analyzed acoustic emission (AE) signals generated during stepwise increases in injection pressure. Frequency analysis of thousands of calibrated AE signals reveals that faultreactivation occurs through the activation of numerous AE source patches withmillimeter-scale radii, far smaller than the fault surface of the sample. Thecumulative area of these reactivated patches exceeds the fault area byapproximately one to two orders of magnitude (~10–50×) during each pressurestep. These results demonstrate that permeability enhancement is not driven bya single large slip event but emerges from the sequential activation andinteraction of multiple slip patches that progressively establish a connectedflow pathway.

name: Guilherme Zakarewicz
title: DAS–Geophone MASW in Permafrost: Lateral Variability and Implications for Subsurface Characterization in a Changing Arctic
authors: Guilherme Zakarewicz^{1}, Gabriel Rocha dos Santos^{1}, Tieyuan Zhu^{1}, Ming Xiao^{2}, Eileen R. Martin^{3}, Ziyi Wang^{4}
institutions:
^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
^{2} Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, The Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA, USA
^{3} Department of Geophysics, Department of Applied Math and Statistics, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
^{4} Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, Colorado School of Mines, Golden, CO, USA
abstract: Permafrost is a subsurface condition wheresoil or rock remains below freezing temperatures for at least two consecutiveyears, covering large portions of the Northern hemisphere and Alaska. However, recent climate changes are accelerating its degradation, resulting insubsidence, riverbank erosion, and infrastructure damage. Detecting andtracking permafrost change remains challenging because many traditionalobservations are expensive and invasive. In this context, geophysical methodsoffer a practical complement by identifying differences in the physicalproperties. For instance, elastic seismic wave speeds respond strongly tovariations in ice and liquid water content.\nIn this study we compare Vs profiles derivedfrom (i) a distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) fiber and (ii) conventionalgeophone arrays at five different locations in Utqiaġvik, Alaska. Since the DASand geophones were not exactly co-located (5-45 meters offset), the comparisonprovides enough lateral separation to test spatial variability. Although somesites presented similar Vs profiles, others showed larger discrepancies, exceeding the uncertainty bounds (typical ΔVs of ~100–400 m/s). We interpret thosedifferences as reflecting lateral heterogeneity at dozen-of-meters scalesrather than differences in the acquisition systems. To provide a quantitativeexample of a physical parameter that could illustrate the observed differences, we apply a rock-physics relation to estimate ice/water volumetric content andquantify how much variability in water saturation would be required to explainthe observed Vs differences (typical ΔSw of ~0.15). We also compare theVs-derived saturation profiles with temperature-based estimates from power-lawrelationships reported by an independent study to check plausibility.\nOur results show that permafrost should not betreated as laterally uniform when constructing velocity models and interpretingtime-lapse changes, especially in coastal polygonal tundra where we expectvariations in ice content, salinity and porosity. Furthermore, spatially densemeasurements are essential for interpreting apparent changes in regions withcomplex cryostructure and hydrology.

name: Ula Filipowicz
title: Modelling the Subduction Interface: The Role of Cohesion in Fault Stability
authors: Urszula Filipowicz^{1}, Donald Fisher^{1}, John Hooker^{2}, Tushar Mittal^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University\n^{2} Department of Atmospheric Science, Environmental Sciences, University of Incarnate Word
abstract: Earthquakes are among the most significantgeohazards on Earth, with the largest events occurring along subduction zones. The mechanisms responsible for unstable slip along megathrust faults arebelieved to be primarily controlled by friction, normal stress, and fluidpressure. These concepts are reflected by earthquake models, which typicallyassume slip follows the rate-and-state friction laws, where friction evolves inresponse to velocity stepping, but cohesion is not included in thecalculations. More recent experimental work, described by the CNS model, hasshown that cohesion might be an important aspect to consider when determiningthe type of failure that will occur along the subduction interface, highlighting how behaviour of faults can be defined from grain-scalemechanisms. Based on this microphysical research whilst also challenging thecurrent paradigm, the hypothesis of this study is that cohesion variations cantrigger fault instabilities independent of velocity weakening.\nIn order to test the role of cohesion, anumerical framework called the MEFISTO (*{Mineralization, Earthquake, and Fluid flow Integrated SimulaTOr}) model will be used. By simplifying theproblem to a zero-dimensional block, the separated effects of cohesion andfriction can be examined and quantified. This will improve MEFISTO’s ability tosimulate earthquake nucleation and strengthening, allowing predictions for howdifferent variables such as temperature and strain rates during interseismicperiods affect cohesion, which can impact slip behaviour and result inearthquakes. Once cohesion is incorporated into the full MEFISTO framework, theresulting forecasts of earthquake size and distribution will be compared withthe Global Centroid Moment Tensor (GCMT) catalogue to evaluate the predictionsof the model, and hence, the significance of cohesion in fault stability. Suchresults would develop understanding of subduction zones and guide futureapplications of the model directly to field observations and laboratoryanalysis.

name: Zach Baran
title: Stratigraphy and Paleohydrology of Fluvial Deposits Near Juventae Chasma in Mars’s Southern Highlands
authors: Zachary J. Baran^{1}, Benjamin T. Cardenas^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Sedimentary basin stratigraphy recordsinformation about a region’s past depositional environments. Ancient fluvialdeposits on Mars are often found within regional or large-scale topographiclows like craters or along the margin of the northern lowlands. However, arecent study showed that abundant fluvial strata also exist in the southernhighlands, suggesting that stratigraphic basins also exist in locationsincongruent with the modern topography. One of these southern highland stratalocations is Juventae Plateau (62.5°W 4.50°S). Previous studies have identifiedhydrated sulfate minerals in strata across the plateau, as well as ancientriver channel deposits, suggesting past water, but stratigraphic relationshipshave not been quantified and a depositional setting to explain both featureshas not been put forward.\nWe used high-resolution satellite images anddigital elevation models to map ridges previously interpreted to be exhumedriver-channel belts based on exposed point-bar structures and stacking patternssimilar to exhumed channel belts on Earth and elsewhere on Mars. We measuredthe thicknesses of layered beds and ridges and found that ridges areconsistently thicker than the layered deposits. The total elevation rangeoccupied by the ridges and layered deposits suggests over 250 meters of basinfill. We measured orientations of strata and found both relatively flat-lyingbeds and inclined, truncated strata, which we interpret as fluvial floodplainand bar deposits respectively. Dip direction and exposed point-bar structuressuggest a paleoflow direction of north-to-south, which is notably opposite tothe modern regional topographic slope.\nWe measured ridge caprock thicknesses toreconstruct paleochannel depths and to look for downstream changes inpaleochannel depth, testing hypotheses for deltaic (downstream thickening) andterminal fan (downstream thinning) channels, further constraining thedepositional setting. Reconstructed channel depths were also used to betterunderstand water availability and climate during basin filling byreconstructing water discharge using established relationships.

name: Olivia DiPrinzio
title: What Factors Drive Farmers’ Climate Risk Perceptions? A case study in Chitwan, Nepal
authors: Olivia DiPrinzio^{1, 2}, Nicolas Choquette-Levy^{1, 2}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2} Earth and Environmental Systems Institute, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Under climate change, global crop yields areprojected to decline significantly, with staple crops showing reductions of upto 10% per degree of warming (°C). Particularly, this reality is most impactfulon socio-economically vulnerable communities, such as farmers in South Asia, whose incomes are predicted to decline by 28% annually on average due toclimate change’s impacts. Concurrently, climate and agricultural policiesworsen existing adverse circumstances by omitting community climate riskperceptions. Such policy frameworks fail to integrate community-specific risks, tolerance, and exposure, thereby threatening livelihoods reliant onagriculture. To date, there is a limited understanding of the effectiveness ofrisk-informed policies under climate change uncertainty, whether in standaloneanalyses or compared with non-risk-informed policies.\nTo address this gap, multivariate statisticalmethods were employed to examine the drivers of farmers’ hazard risk perceptionin Chitwan, one of Nepal’s most climate-vulnerable regions, using a 2022survey. Guiding this process, causal modeling identified three key feedbackmechanisms hypothesized to govern farmers’ reported exposure: insurance levels, remittance income, and perspectives on farming as a livelihood strategy. Initial statistical analysis demonstrates the importance of groundwater andirrigation accessibility, the varied influence of demographic variables, andremittances’ minimal influence on the frequency of self-reported exposure toclimate-influenced hazards, the last of which contradicts the proposedhypothesis of remittances’ impact. Our results demonstrate inherent variabilityin hazard perceptions, such that while certain drivers are relevant across allhazards, a more tailored approach to driver consideration is required. Consequently, a signal exists for hazard-specific policies, such ashazard-specific vulnerability indices. As these are initial results, next stepsinclude statistical analysis of farmers’ perceptions of future risks, time-series analysis to provide a more nuanced view of variability inperceptions, self-reports compared against climatological data (e. g. SPEI), andan exploration of hazard-specific exposure policies.

name: Jasmine Walker
title: The Role of Fine Sediment in Channel Mobility Stratigraphic Architecture
authors: Jasmine Walker^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Understanding how fluvial systems respond tochange and record the history of landscape changes is essential for sustainablymanaging ecosystems, remediating environmental contaminants, efficientlyexploring for natural resources, and successfully mitigating risks associatedwith river movements and floodplain inundation. Rivers play a key role inshaping the modern landscapes we inhabit and the buried deposits that formstratigraphy, from which we interpret the history of surface conditions on Earth. The integrated effect of silts and clays on fluvial landscape dynamicsis recorded in the stratigraphic architecture of ancient river deposits and canenhance or occlude fluid flow in buried aquifers and reservoirs. Understandinghow fine-sediment supply impacts channel mobility, stratigraphic architecture, and subsurface fluid flow is, therefore, key for reconstructing paleo-landscapeconditions and predicting the distribution and connectivity of subsurfacereservoirs, aquifers, and potential geothermal and carbon storage sites.\nA key challenge in understanding therelationship between the supply of fine sediment and resulting stratigraphicarchitecture is the interplay between processes occurring at both spatially andtemporally variable scales. I aim to close this gap through inquiry into modernrivers and ancient river deposits that assess the role of fine sediment inchannel mobility and long-term channel stratigraphic architecture, or“stacking”, in sedimentary basins. Using a combination of remote sensing ofmodern rivers, subsurface (seismic and well log) observations of ancient riverdeposits, and numerical modeling, I propose to answer the following sciencequestions: (1) How does suspended-sediment supply impact channel mobility inglobal alluvial rivers? (2) What is the relationship between fine-sedimentsupply, channel mobility, and channel-belt depositional architecture influvio-deltaic settings?

name: Ran He
title: Iron carbonate as a robust archive forreducing paleoenvironmental conditions: oxygen and clumped isotopes evidencefrom burial diagenesis
authors: Ran He^{1}, Max K. Lloyd^{1}, Brian Currie^{2}, Miquela Ingalls^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2} Department of Geology and Environmental Earth Science, Miami University, Oxford, OH, USA
abstract: Siderite (FeCO_{3}) is aredox-sensitive carbonate mineral that is pervasive in the rock record and canenable reconstructions of ancient reducing environments on Earth and Mars. However, post-depositional processes like burial diagenesis and surficialweathering can alter primary isotopic signatures through dissolution andreprecipitation (δ^{13}C, δ^{18}O and T(∆_{47}), limiting the reliability of these proxies. Unlike calcite and dolomite, thesusceptibility of isotopic clumping in siderite to overprinting by theseprocesses is poorly understood. We hypothesize that siderite is more resistantto these processes than calcite during fluid-mediated diagenesis due to itslower solubility. To test this hypothesis, we analyzed siderite and calcitesamples from the Paleocene Fort Union Formation in the Wind River Basin, Wyoming. We collected coeval terrestrial siderite concretions and cement fromtwo outcrops and six drill cores spanning a range of maximum burial depths (1.5-3.5km) due to tectonics, allowing us to distinguish between water-rockalteration during burial diagenesis and surficial weathering.\nAll calcite samples yield elevated T(∆_{47}) temperatures (44.5±1.2°C to 55.9±2.6 °C) paired with low and variable δ^{18} Ovalues (-18.9 to -11.2‰), whereas siderite from outcrops and shallow coresrecords plausible Earth surface temperatures (9.1^{+5.7}/_{-5.4}°C to 27.6^{+5}/_{-4.8} °C). °C). Two micritic siderite ∆_{47}from deepest core (3.5 km burial) however, shows elevated T(∆_{47}) temperatures (43.7±0.9°C to 60.2^{+4.9}/_{-4.7} °C), indicatingresetting through recrystallization. Of these two altered siderite samples, oneexhibits textural and chemical evidence of recrystallization during burialunder scanning electron microscopy, while the other shows no petrographic signsof alteration. Combining T(∆_{47}) and δ^{18}O, water-rockinteraction model suggests the altered siderite has experienced rock-buffereddiagenesis (water-to-rock ratio<0.5), whereas calcite has experiencedfluid-buffered diagenesis (water-to-rock ratio>1). Together, these resultsdemonstrate that siderite δ^{18}O and T(∆_{47}) are more robustto burial alteration than calcite, highlighting the potential of siderite as areliable proxy for ancient reducing aqueous environments.

name: Yusuke Kubota
title: The role of the mantle decompaction layerin Hadean volcanism
authors: Yusuke Kubota^{1}, John Rudge^{2}, Bradford Foley^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University\n^{2} Department of Earth Sciences, University of Cambridge
abstract:
How the very early Earth lost its internalheat remains a subject of debate. Early Earth may have been characterized byextensive magmatism due to a hot mantle, which then acted as the primary heatloss mechanism, or been more volcanically quiescent, where heat conductionthrough the lithosphere served as the primary heat loss mechanism. The primarymode of early Earth heat loss would then strongly influence tectonics and crustformation, the long-term thermal evolution of the interior, and surface environmentswhere life could originate in the Hadean or Eoarchean.
Our recent crustal evolution model suggeststhat mantle melt production and mafic extrusive volcanism must have beenlimited prior to 3.6 Ga to remain consistent with Hf isotope data. Wehypothesized that these geochemical constraints require a 'quiescent Earth'with a low melt production rate (<0.6 mm/yr). However, the actual magmasupply is governed by complex geodynamic factors: specifically, the mechanicsof melt generation, ascent, and accumulation at the mantle-crust boundary. Understanding these physical mechanisms is critical, particularly whenevaluating high-flux regimes such as heat-pipe tectonics, which may beincompatible with the low rates inferred from the geochemical record.
A critical phenomenon affecting this supply isthe formation of a decompaction layer beneath the mantle-crust interface. Sincethe crust acts as a rigid thermal boundary, temperatures drop rapidly near thisinterface. Consequently, ascending melt encounters a freezing horizon that actsas a permeability barrier, causing it to accumulate. Within this zone, thedecompaction layer and accumulated magma generate significant melt overpressurerelative to the solid matrix, driving magma into the plumbing system andinitiating ascent. Therefore, characterizing the dynamics of the decompactionlayer is crucial for understanding the physical controls on melt supply.
Recent numerical modeling of Io, an activeheat-pipe body, demonstrates that crustal thermal structure is controlled bythe physics of two-phase melt transport. This model suggests that magmatransport is driven by mantle overpressure at the decompaction layer butlimited by solidification within the plumbing system. Applying this physicalframework to the Hadean, we tested which mantle dynamics and temperature rangesare compatible with the restricted melt fluxes required by the geochemicalrecord. Preliminary results demonstrate the existence of a decompaction layer, where both effective pressure and extraction rates increase significantly withporosity. By systematically exploring the parameter space, we identify thespecific mantle geodynamic conditions required to align plateau meltingtectonics with the Hf isotope constraints.

name: Oliver Neilson
title: Quantifying the timing and volume ofvolcanic degassing in deep time: A case study from the Sinemurian –Pliensbachian Boundary Event
authors: Oliver Neilson^{1}, Isabel M. Fendley^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Pennsylvania State University, State College, PA, USA
abstract:
Understanding deep-time climatic perturbationsrelies on quantifying the initial drivers them. Earth system perturbations arehighly sensitive to, among other parameters, the timing and duration ofvolcanic degassing. Currently, these parameters are coarsely constrained, withvolatile estimates coming from melt inclusion data and radiometric dating^{1}.However, recent work has highlighted the power of combining sedimentary mercury (Hg), a volcanic tracer, and Hg cycle box models to estimate the tempo and volumeof volcanic degassing in deep time^{2}.
Here, we present a quantitativehigh-resolution degassing history through the Sinemurian - Pliensbachian Boundary Event (SPBE). This protracted negative “U-shaped” carbon isotopeexcursion lasted for over 4 million years in the Early Jurassic (ca. 190 Ma). We utilise over 1600 samples collected from the recently drilled core at Prees, Cheshire Basin, U. K., as part of the International Continental Scientific Drilling Program JET project.
The SPBE is broadly coeval with increasedrifting from the break-up of Pangea, the opening of the Hispanic Seaway, and apulse of volcanic activity from the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province^{3–5}, all of which may have contributed to its shape and duration. We quantify thetempo and volume of volcanic degassing during the SPBE using a geochemicalmachine-learning framework to isolate volcanically sourced Hg, followed byidentification of the best-fit degassing scenarios using a global Hg box model. To see how this would affect the carbon isotope record, we use the best-fitdegassing scenario as an input to a carbon cycle model. We compare the modelledrecord to the observed record and discuss major differences.
This novel method allows for a clearer pictureof past climatic feedbacks and Earth system dynamics; quantifying past climaticchanges and their drivers are essential for better contextualising modern andfuture climate change.

name: Samuel Williams
title: Quantifyingsediment storage and evacuation in response to compound earthquake and typhoonhazards in the Liwu River, Taiwan
authors: Samuel Williams^{1}, Eric Kirby^{1}, Roman DiBiase^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: In steep, tectonically active landscapes, earthquakes and precipitation can generate large, episodic sediment pulses thattransiently alter channel morphology. The timescales over which these pulsesare evacuated, and the sensitivity of transport to large discharge events, remain uncertain. Understanding how sediment pulsespropagate through boulder-dominated rivers is necessary for predicting thelong-term evolution of active mountain belts. Because these transient responsesinfluence channel longitudinal profiles and the pace at which rivers adjust totectonic forcing, constraints on sediment storage and evacuation are essentialfor linking short-term events to long-term landscape evolution. A natural experiment is posed by the Liwu River following the 2024Hualien earthquake in the Central Range of Taiwan. This Mw 7.2 event triggeredwidespread co-seismic landsliding, and an intense subsequent typhoon season hadmultiple storms capable of triggering additional landsliding and mobilizingstored sediment. I will quantify spatial and temporal patterns of sedimentstorage and evacuation in the Liwu River using a multi-temporal dataset to testthe following hypotheses: (1) sediment aggradation will be clustered downstreamof major landslide and tributary inputs rather than uniformly distributed alongthe reach, and (2) reaches with greater pre-event boulder cover will retainsediment longer during floods.\nThis study leverages a high-resolution Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) survey conducted in 2023 that providescentimeter-scale orthophotos and 3D point clouds for baseline channelmorphology. These data will be integrated with a time series of 10–50 cm scaleresolution orthophotos and a repeat UAV survey to quantify bed elevationchange, sediment storage, and boulder exposure from 2023-2026 across a ~4 kmreach of the Liwu River. Together, these observations will provide newconstraints on sediment residence time and the role of boulder cover incontrolling sediment transport following extreme disturbances.

name: Chandan Sahu
title: How does composition variation affectmantle solidus and thermal evolution of rocky planets?
authors: Chandan Sahu^{1}, Bradford Foley^{1}, Aaron Wolf^{2}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}SETI Institute, Mountain View, CA, USA
abstract: Understanding exoplanet interiors remains achallenge due to the inherent difficulty of direct observation. While theiratmospheres are observed using advanced telescopes, interior modeling providesinformation about their interior structure, composition, and evolution relevantfor interpreting atmospheric observations. Current models often assume an Earth-like mineralogy, however rocky exoplanets can come in ranges of differentcompositions. Studies from the Hypatia catalog and other stellar composition cataloguesshow that stars can have a wide range of elemental abundances, leading todiverse mineral compositions in terrestrial planets, as they reflect therefractory materials present in the host star.\nOur research investigates how variations ininterior composition affect the mantle mineralogy and solidus, the viscosityand consequently the planet’s thermal history. The solidus, marking the onsetof melting, is crucial for heat and melt transport. On Earth, olivine andpyroxene are the primary minerals in the upper mantle. Variability in elementalabundances in stars suggests planets may have diverse olivine-pyroxene (Ol-Px) ratios. We use the MELTS model to determine how different mineralogies affectthe mantle's solidus profile. Our results indicate higher solidus temperaturesfor higher Ol-Px ratio. We then integrate the calculated solidii with themantle adiabat and heat sources/sinks to simulate interactions between mantlecomposition, temperature, viscosity, and lid growth over geological timescales. We also model the viscosity using flow laws and creep mechanisms, to observethe behaviour with changing Ol-Px ratio. This helps us understand meltproduction, outgassing, volcanism, and other dynamic processes during a rockyplanet’s evolution, aiding in predicting the thermal and geological history ofexoplanets. Understanding these is essential for identifying the presence oftectonic activity and volcanism, and can create and sustain habitable conditions.

name: Christian Lundy
title: The Stabilization of Wastewater-Derived Phosphorus in a Florida Keys, USA Karstic Aquifer
authors: Christian Lundy^{1}, Eleanor Spielman-Sun^{2}, Lee Kump^{1}, Miquela Ingalls^{1}, and Rachel Housego^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}SLACNational Accelerator Laboratory, 2575 Sand Hill Road, Menlo Park, CA, USA
abstract: Submarinegroundwater discharge is an often overlooked source of nutrient loading incoastal ecosystems. Phosphorus (P) inputs into ocean surface waters can causeeutrophication, leading to algal blooms and deoxygenation. Shallow wastewaterinjection in Marathon, FL injects up to 700, 000 liters of high-P treatedwastewater daily approximately 30 meters into the Key Largo Limestone (KLL) aquifer for disposal. P concentrations are greatly decreased within the plumedue to dilution, adsorption of P to the calcite lattice, and precipitation of Pminerals. This P sink is under threat as rising sea levels cause salineintrusion into previously fresh aquifer regions, leading to P desorption andpossible P mineral dissolution. This study aims to characterize the P mineralsprecipitated from KLL shallow wastewater injection to assess P sink stabilityunder future saline intrusion scenarios.\nCarbonatecores were collected at three locations along a cross-island transect throughthe Marathon wastewater plume in September 2025. Adjacent monitoring wells wereinstrumented with conductivity-temperature-depth sensors to determine coresalinity zones and water samples were collected for plume geochemicalcharacterization. Thin sections from the cores were selected from fresh andsaline aquifer regions and sections of varying secondary porosity. They will beanalyzed using µ-X-Ray Absorbance Near Edge Structures (µ-XANES) and µ-X-Ray Fluorescence (µ-XRF) at the Stanford Synchrotron Radiation Lightsource (SSRL) and Scanning Electron Microscopy/Energy Dispersive Spectroscopy (SEM/EDS) atthe Penn State Materials Characterization Laboratory to determine P mineralspeciation. We hypothesize that more stable P minerals will be present inaquifer regions with lower salinity and less secondary porosity, as decreasedgroundwater residence time from preferential karstic pathways leads todecreased P mineral precipitation. This project holds important implicationsfor P loading under future saline intrusion scenarios and can provide importantgeochemical constraints for reactive transport modeling of shallow wastewaterinjection.

name: Anthony Delgadillo Salas de la Tierra
title: Reconstructing Late Pleistocene/Holocene Fire–Vegetation–Human Feedback in the Lake Malawi Basin Using Core MAL05-2A
authors: Anthony Delgadillo Salas de la Tierra^{1}, Sarah Ivory^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Lake Malawi is an important sedimentaryarchive for understanding the long-term changes between tropical Africanclimate, ecosystems, and early human activity. During the Pleistocene, East Africa experienced megadroughts causing permanent ecological reorganizationbetween ~85-70 ka, shifting from Afromontane forests to miombo woodlands. It is unclear if the transition issolely a climate shift or if early anthropogenic fire-vegetation feedbackoccurred. Addressing this gap has been challenging due to chronologicaluncertainties and coarse sampling resolutions during the Late Pleistocene-Holocene transition. This project tests the hypothesis that earlyhuman fire use during the 85-70 ka transition created self-sustained ecologicalfeedback that later intensified during the Holocene agropastoralism.\nThisproject aims to analyze 56 sediment samples from core MAL05-2A, spanning thelast ~123, 000 years with some intervals studied at a higher resolution such asa millennial scale. By utilizing pollen analysis to track vegetation changeswith microscopic charcoal analysis to measure fire activity, this study willdevelop an improved understanding of environmental conditions in southeast Africa. Results are expected to reveal two major phases of fireintensification, the ~85-70ka transition and the Holocene. This fireintensification is suspected to be characterized by a continuous directionalshift toward grass dominated savanna assemblages. This research aims todetermine whether fire-maintained landscapes in Southeast Africa are a modernoccurrence or a legacy of Pleistocene anthropogenic influence, providing abaseline for understanding modern landscape degradation and ecosystemresilience under climate change.

name: Zach Loveall
title: Dual-Clumped Isotope Disequilibrium in Terrestrial Carbonates
authors: Zachary Loveall^{1}, Ellen Olsen^{1}, Miquela Ingalls^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Terrestrial carbonates preserve valuablepaleoclimate records in their isotopic compositions. However, kinetic effectsassociated with dissolved inorganic carbon cycling, including CO_{2}degassing, absorption, and water mixing can shift isotopic systems out ofequilibrium. Because isotopic equilibration in the DIC–H_{2}O systemoccurs over hours to days, rapidly forming carbonates may preserve transientdisequilibrium signals, complicating paleoclimate records. Carbonates from the Green River Formation of Wyoming and Utah record lacustrine, wetland, andshoreline environments during the Early Eocene Climatic Optimum, a warminterval characterized by elevated pCO_{2} and high temperatures. Thesedeposits provide an ideal natural laboratory for evaluating how rapid carbonateprecipitation records isotopic disequilibrium across terrestrial environmentsand facies. Petrographic screening and mineralogical analyses were conducted onstratigraphically constrained samples to assess diagenetic overprinting. Weinterpreted preliminary δ^{13}C, δ^{18}O, and dual-clumpedisotope (Δ_{47}–Δ_{48}) values within the context ofdepositional and diagenetic history to characterize departures fromthermodynamic equilibrium. Preliminary petrographic characterization andinitial dual-clumped results suggest variability among facies that may reflectformation mechanisms rather than temperature alone. These results will refineinterpretations of carbonate-based paleotemperature reconstructions andestablish a framework for identifying and quantifying isotopic disequilibriumin terrestrial systems during past greenhouse climates.

name: Lara Williams
title: Investigating deep critical zone structureusing landslide scars in the Taiwan Central Range
authors: Lara Williams^{1}, Roman A DiBiase^{1, 2}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2} Earth and Environmental Systems Institute, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: The Critical Zone (CZ) is the near-subsurfacelayer that integrates rock, water, air, and biotic processes; it is wherebedrock is weathered and regolith is produced. The thickness of this weatheredzone is dependent on lithology, climate, and erosion rate. Models indicate thatweathering depths will be deeper in areas of slower erosion, as slower erosionrates will increase soil residence times and allow for deeper propagation ofweathering. However, it is difficult to isolate the influence of individual factors, and the lower boundary of the CZ is difficult to study as it is often beneathtens of meters of weathered material.\nTo address these challenges and isolate therole of erosion in determining weathering depth, I plan to examine landslidescars in the Central Range of Taiwan that provide a unique window into thesubsurface. The steep, rapidly eroding Central Range has a consistent climateand lithology, with landslides cutting directly into small patches of lowrelief topography found along the spine of the range. These landslide scarsoften expose the full depth of the weathered zone and extend into unalteredbedrock below. I plan to measure the depth of weathering in these scars usingaerial photography and high-quality drone imagery obtained in 2024 from Mt. Qilai from which I will build 3D models of the topography. By using the slopeof the low relief surfaces as a proxy for erosion rate, this will provide afirst-order sense of how weathering depth responds to erosion.

name: Tsunami Sharmba
title: A Network Analysis of Administrative Callsand User Interdependencies in the Colorado River Basin
authors: Tsunami Sharmba^{1}, Dr. Antonia Hadjimichael^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: The Colorado River sustains over 40 millionpeople, 5 million acres of cropland, and a $1.4 trillion economy across sevenU. S. states and Mexico. The basin faces mounting stress from chronicoverallocation, prolonged drought, and accelerating climate change. Initialwater allocations were based on flow estimates that exceeded actual averages byat least 3 million acre-feet, a structural deficit that has deepened as warmingtemperatures reduce snowpack and accelerate evaporation. As supply and demanddiverge, the basin is approaching a governance crisis that current frameworksare ill-equipped to address.\nUnder prior appropriation, senior water rightsholders place administrative calls that curtail junior users during scarcity. These calls are the operational backbone of the system, but the patterns theyproduce regarding who curtails whom, how often, for how long, and under whathydrological conditions, reveal how climate stress propagates unevenly across arigid, seniority-bound network of interdependent users. When one user's callrestricts another, that stress can trigger broader adaptive responses such aswater transactions, crop changes, and decisions that carry their own risks andtradeoffs. Understanding where those pressures concentrate and how they cascadeis essential for anticipating maladaptation before it locks in.\nThis research maps the structure of water userinterdependencies in the Colorado River Basin using administrative call recordsfrom the Colorado Division of Water Resources. By representing users as anetwork, this work identifies which users and reaches are most vulnerable tocascading curtailment and where the system is most delicate. These findingswill inform future efforts to build resilience into governance frameworks amida deeply uncertain and changing climate.

name: Jackson Saftner
title: Low-Cost Monitoring of Inert Gas Stimulation with DAS
authors: Jackson Saftner^{1}, Xinxin He^{2}, Tieyuan Zhu^{1}, Shimin Liu^{2}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2} Department of Energy and Mineral Engineering, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: High-density microseismic monitoring is aproven tool for stimulation verification and reservoir surveillance, butconventional campaigns typically require a dedicated monitoring well or a largesurface geophone array. Here, we evaluate distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) asa cost-effective alternative by analyzing a continuous dataset acquired duringan inert-gas (liquid CO₂) stimulation at an onshore well site near Olean, New York.\nThe dataset was recorded on a fiber arrayattached to the same wireline used to deploy the stimulation tool to the targetinterval. This single-well setup avoids an additional monitoring well and stillprovides dense, high-sensitivity measurements. In the continuous record, wecapture the stimulation pulse with high signal-to-noise ratio and a richpost-stimulation interval characterized by sustained changes in seismic energyand numerous broadband impulsive signals consistent with cracking or deformationepisodes.\nTo enable rapid diagnostics, we develop alightweight detection workflow based on multi-band energy attributes andSTA/LTA triggering. Applying the workflow, we identify 732 candidate impulsiveevents and track the post-stimulation event-rate evolution, finding an Omori-type decay similar to earthquake aftershocks. We then add a simplesource-location step to estimate first-pass locations for a subset ofdetections (58 events), providing stimulation-verification metrics thatindicate fracture propagation to approximately 50 m from the stimulation well.

name: Gabriel Dos Santos
title: Distributed Sensing of Frost Quakes and Ice-Wedge Cracking in Utqiaġvik, Alaska
authors: Gabriel Rocha dos Santos^{1}, Tieyuan Zhu^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Ice wedge polygons are distinctive periglaciallandforms that result from repeated cycles of ground contraction and crackinfilling in permafrost terrains.
