However, the fracture events that initiatetheir growth remain poorly documented through direct field observations. Inthis study, we analyze thousands of short-duration seismic events recorded overtwo winters using continuous Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) in Utqiaġvik, Alaska. These events display clear body wave arrivals followed by dominant surfacewave energy and broadband high-frequency content, suggesting shallow sourcesnear the fiber. We found a strong correspondence between peaks in seismicactivity and peaks in modeled ground thermal stress, derived from athermo-viscoelastic model constrained by Distributed Temperature Sensing (DTS) from a co-located fiber. These signals are interpreted as cryoseisms resultingfrom the thermal cracking of ice wedges during periods of intense groundcooling, commonly referred to as frost quakes. To investigate the spatialvariability of these events, we apply Matched Field Processing (MFP) using bothsurface and body wave arrivals. The resulting maps reveal evolving fracturepatterns across the tundra surface. In addition, we performed source mechanisminversion on a subset of near-field events to investigate whether theirwaveforms can be used to infer rupture orientation or mode. Our resultsdemonstrate the utility of DAS and DTS for detecting and characterizingthermally induced fracturing in permafrost. By combining seismic and thermalanalyses, we provide new insights into the seasonal evolution of subsurfacecracking and ice wedge development in a rapidly changing Arctic climate.

name: Dayang Zhou
title: Listening to Arctic Sea Ice: Seismic Tremors as a Proxy for Ice Strength
authors: Dayang Zhou^{1}, Gabriel Rocha dos Santos^{1}, Jackson Saftner^{1}, Tieyuan Zhu^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Sea ice is a critical component of the polarsystem, supporting Arctic ecosystems and coastal communities, reflecting asubstantial fraction of incoming solar radiation, and attenuating ocean waveenergy by acting as a mechanical buffer along coastlines. Under ongoing climatewarming, Arctic sea-ice extent has declined rapidly. Reduced ice coverincreases coastal exposure to wave forcing, accelerating erosion andheightening the vulnerability of infrastructure and communities. Monitoringnearshore sea-ice stability is therefore essential for assessing coastalhazards and environmental change in the Arctic.\nIn contrast to remote sensing methods, whichtypically provide spatial resolutions of tens of kilometers and temporalresolutions of days to weeks, seismic observations offer continuous, high-temporal-resolution monitoring that operates reliably through polar nightand severe weather. Seismic data are particularly sensitive to mechanical iceprocesses that are difficult to observe directly. Interactions between driftingpack ice and landfast ice generate distinctive harmonic tremor signals that canbe separated from other seismic sources. In this study, we investigate thephysical processes responsible for these harmonic features and explore theirrelationship to landfast-ice extent through analysis of fundamentalfrequencies.\nTo enable systematic detection, we apply amachine learning approach based on YOLO (You Only Look Once) to identifyharmonic signals in the time–frequency domain. The detected events exhibitclear seasonal variability, suggesting strong links to the evolving state ofnearshore sea ice. These results demonstrate the potential of seismicmonitoring combined with machine learning to provide new constraints on coastalsea-ice dynamics.

name: Young Kim
title: Assessing Post‑Collapse Flank Instabilityat Anak Krakatau Using Satellite Remote Sensing
authors: Young Cheol Kim^{1}, Christelle Wauthier^{1, 2}, Thomas R. Walter^{3}, Semeidi Husrin^{4}, Herlan Darmawan^{5}, Daniel Müller^{3}
institutions:
^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
^{2} Institute for Computational and Data Science, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
^{3}GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences, Helmholtz Centre Potsdam, Telegrafenberg Potsdam, Germany
^{4} The National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN), Indonesia, Jakarta, Indonesia
^{5} Laboratory of Geophysics, Department of Physics, Facultyof Mathematics and Natural Sciences, Universitas Gadjah Mada, Yogyakarta, Indonesia
abstract: Anak Krakatau Volcano, Indonesia, experienceda major flank collapse on December 22, 2018, generating a tsunami that causedsignificant casualties. Prior InSAR studies showed more than a decade ofinstability on the southwest flank. This study investigates whether instability continued after the 2018 event. We used ALOS-2 and Sentinel-1 data spanning2019 to 2024. Due to ongoing eruptive activity and surface changes, threeseparate time-series were generated to ensure enough reliable pixels for InSARtime-series analysis. The key focus area was the southwest part of Anak Krakatau, where faster movement was observed prior to the collapse and most ofthe newly erupted material had accumulated.\nPost-collapse displacements show a stronggradient that aligns with fractures observed in drone imagery. To betterinterpret motion, we decomposed the InSAR time series into vertical andeast–west components, excluding the north–south direction due to lowsensitivity. The vertical displacement shows an exponential decay pattern, interpreted as compaction and consolidation of fresh deposits. To avoid thissignal dominating source modeling, we limited geodetic modeling to laterintervals of the time series. These displacements were then used in rectangulardislocation inversions to characterize the subsurface processes controllingpost-collapse deformation.

name: Sierra Melton
title: Enhanced Grounding Zone Stresses at an Ice Cliff Compared to at a Freely Spreading Ice Shelf
authors: Sierra Melton^{1}, Byron Parizek^{1, 2}, Richard Alley^{1}, Sridhar Anandakrishnan^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, and Earth and Environmental Systems Institute, Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2} Mathematicsand Geoscience, Pennsylvania State University, DuBois, PA, USA
abstract: Ice stored in the Greenland and Antarctic Ice Sheets largely flows to the ocean through fast-flowing outlet glaciers and icestreams, forming floating ice shelves when it crosses the grounding zone. Iceshelves are susceptible to melting, rifting, and collapse, which has beenobserved to speed flow of non-floating ice and to expose grounded ice cliffsthat can retreat rapidly by iceberg calving, raising sea level. Most ice sheetmodels do not simulate coupled ice-shelf loss and calving-cliff retreat becauseof difficulty in modeling the governing processes at suitable spatiotemporalresolutions and parameterizing the sub-gridscale physics involved in thesetransition regions. With the Ice-sheet and Sea-level System Model (ISSM), wecompare the 3D grounding zone stresses for a freely spreading ice shelf withthose at an ice cliff for an idealized outlet glacier. At an ice cliff, lack ofsupport from any further glacial ice in the down-flow direction causes a stressimbalance, compensated for by enhanced englacial stresses. These enhancedstresses should speed rates of glacial thinning and retreat for an ice cliffcompared to a freely spreading shelf because they are occurring within thegrounding zone rather than within the distal zones of the attached ice shelf. Even a freely spreading ice shelf underestimates cliff stresses by shiftingstresses from the grounding line to the front of the shelf. Our results willultimately help represent ice-cliff retreat more accurately in ice sheet modelsto improve sea-level rise projections.

name: Noshin Sharmili
title: Exploring the Depositional & Erosional Morphology of Jezero Crater
authors: Noshin Sharmili^{1}, Liz Hajek^{1}, Kathryn Stack Morgan^{2}, Ben Cardenas^{1}, Libby Ives^{3}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, CA\n^{3} Michigan Geological Survey, Kalamazoo, MI
abstract: The Jezero crater western fan, an explorationsite of the Mars 2020 Perseverance rover, contains a record ofpaleoenvironmental conditions, sedimentary processes, and potentialbiosignatures. It has generally been assumed that the modern shape and extentof the Jezero western fan is the result of the interplay between a deltaicdeposit and billions of years of wind erosion on the Martian surface. Finegrained facies such as silt and clay would have been preferentially removed bywind erosion while rocks made of sand and gravel would have been more likely tobe preserved.\nHowever, this hypothesis is not consistentwith the modern shape and extent of the Jezero western fan. Specifically, thescarp that defines the current extent of the western fan is abrupt and does notcoincide with a downstream decrease in grain size. Instead, observations madeduring Perseverance’s traverse across the crater floor and the Jezero craterwestern fan suggest that the strongest control on the present shape of the fanis the spatial distribution of a sandstone- and boulder-bearing sequence (“the Upper Fan group”) that is unconformably overlain on underlying fluvial anddeltaic sediments and absent on crater floor. Boulders are impervious to winderosion and would essentially armor any underlying sedimentary rocks fromerosion. This study employed numerical models to investigate the factorscontributing to the preservation of Jezero Crater’s western fan morphology andto understand the erosion rates affecting its formation and evolution. Theexperiments tested the hypothesis that the fan's shape was originally inheritedfrom the lower Otis Peak Formation and later preserved by the erosion-resistantigneous boulder deposits of the upper Otis Peak Formation.

name: Caleb Norville
title: Impacts of Fire and Solar Radiation on Afroalpine Vegetation in the Rwenzori Mountains
authors: Caleb Norville^{1}, Sarah Ivory^{1, 2}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2}EESI, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract: Previous work has elucidated the responses of Rwenzori Mountains Afroalpine vegetation to Holocene temperature andprecipitation changes, suggesting that Afroalpine ecologies may be moreinsulated from the impacts of increasing temperature than lower Afromontaneforest communities. Precipitation changes over the Holocene seem to correlatemore closely to observed changes in vegetation recorded by pollen preserved in Afroalpine lakes. However, a large portion of the variance in the pollen dataremains unexplained by these climate factors, necessitating the examination ofother environmental or ecological factors as potential drivers of vegetation. Fire has been proposed as a major catalyst for rapid vegetation change in the Afroalpine zone, especially following a large wildfire in 2012. However, recentwork has suggested that large Afroalpine fires were rare to absent across mostof the Holocene, making the 2012 event unprecedented over the past 13 ka. Ongoing work is focused on understanding the record of vegetation response tothis localized recent fire event.\nAfroalpine elevations produce harsh conditionsfor plants, where frequent cloud cover and frost limits plant growth, and highUV-B influxes necessitate adaptations to this damaging solar radiation. Plantsactively respond to changing UV-B influxes during the growing season byregulating their production of protective UV-B absorbing compounds (UACs) whichhave been shown to be well preserved within fossil pollen grains. These UACs inselected pollen taxa can be quantified using micro-FTIR spectroscopy, providinga pollen-based proxy for paleo UV-B influx. Changes in fossil pollen UACs cantrack orbitally controlled changes in solar insolation; however, the impacts ofUV-B blocking cloud cover have yet to be examined. Ongoing work is focused ondetermining whether changes in cloud cover associated with the termination ofthe African Humid Period can be observed in fossil Afroalpine pollen, potentially providing a novel proxy for paleo cloud cover.

name: Eric Hasegawa
title: The effect of ring substitutions onaromatic carboxyl oxygen isotope geochemistry and applications tomacromolecular systems
authors: Eric Hasegawa^{1}, Jason Boettger^{2}, Katherine Dawson^{3}, Katherine Freeman^{1}, Max Lloyd^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2} North Carolina Department of Environmental Quality, Raleigh, NC, USA\n^{3} Department of Environmental Sciences, Rutgers University, Newark, NJ, USA
abstract: The position-specific oxygen isotopegeochemistry of macromolecules such as lignin, kerogen, or meteoritic insolubleorganic matter (IOM) can give insight into the origins and reaction pathways ofdifferent functional groups. These functional groups are dominantly associatedwith aromatic moieties in the macromolecular structures. However, it is unclearif and how functional group electronic properties differ due to substitutionson aromatic rings and how they result in different isotope geochemistry. An exampleis the oxygen exchange chemistry that can occur on an aromatic carboxyl groupsuch as the one found in benzoic acid. In this case, the carbon is sp^{2}hybridized, which links the oxygen to the larger aromatic framework. We aim toanswer the question: how do additional ring substitutions change the oxygenisotopic exchange chemistry at the carboxyl site, and how does this affect ourinterpretation of carboxyl group chemistry in natural samples? Initial densityfunctional theory modeling suggests little to no difference in fractionationfactors, and we follow these studies with physical equilibration experimentsusing methods developed in our previous study of phenol-water oxygen exchange. We reacted benzoic acid and vanillic acid with waters of known oxygen isotopiccompositions at elevated temperatures, and we injected these solutions into ourelectrospray ionization-Orbitrap mass spectrometer to determine oxygenequilibrium fractionation factors (the difference between an equilibratedcarboxyl group’s isotopic composition and the water’s isotopic composition) forthese two molecules. Carboxyl groups can exchange their oxygen in low pHconditions, and therefore their isotopic composition, once corrected with afractionation factor, will likely represent the isotopic composition of thelast acidic alteration fluid to which they were exposed. The impact ofadditional aromatic functional groups will be used as an analog to betterunderstand the impact of aromatic linkages in macromolecular frameworks.

name: Erik Schoonover
title: Linking Arc Granitoids to Ore Deposits through Fluid–Melt–Rock Interactions
authors: Erik Schoonover^{1}, Cole J. Stern^{1}, Renan Beckman^{1}, Rory Changleng^{1}, Evan Ritchey^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
abstract:
Rising demand for key metals has placedincreased focus on discovering new deposits in Earth's crust. Resources, suchas Fe, Cu, and the rare earth elements, are fundamental for infrastructure, energy systems, and national security. Generating deposits large enough to beeconomically viable requires efficient crustal processes that mobilize andconcentrate these metals of interest. Investigating the mechanisms ofore-forming processes is important, particularly, for developing newexploration targets and reducing the economic costs associated with orediscovery and characterization. Crustal ore deposits provide a partial view ofthese processes because they are the final product of multistage, complexprocesses. Deposits are often overprinted by successive mineralization events, strongly modified by post-emplacement alteration, and their source rocks arerarely preserved or exposed. As a result, the physical and chemical mechanismsof ore formation are difficult to observe directly.
Bridging this gap in deposit formationrequires shifting focus from the mineralized deposits to the magmaticenvironments that generate them. Two major deposit types that supply strategicand critical elements are iron oxide-apatite (IOA) and iron oxide-copper-gold (IOCG) deposits. These deposits are exemplar models for metal concentration andmobilization from arc magmas. Competing models for these deposits suggesteither that enrichment occurs through separation of an Fe-rich immiscible meltor through Cl-rich fluid flux that sequester metals from a crystal-rich magma. Therefore, without source context, the interactions and relative rolesof fluid, melt, and magmatic rocks during metal concentration remainsunresolved.
My current hypothesis is that metal-enriched, channel-like features in arc granitoids represent the preserved record of metalmobilization during the magmatic-hydrothermal transition.
These featurescould provide a means to directly link late-stage arc magmatism withore-forming processes. The Tuolumne Intrusive Suite (TIS), CA, USA is an idealsetting, enabling clear observation of the parameters governing fluid-melt-rockinteraction during the metal mobilization.

name: Emma Hartke
title: Holoceneclimate changes, ecosystem conditions & early human activity in the Central Mediterranean: a multi-proxy investigation
authors: Emma Hartke^{1}, Kate Freeman^{1}, Miquela Ingalls^{1}, Melissa Berke^{2}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2} Civil and Environmental Engineering and Earth Sciences, Notre Dame University, Notre Dame, IN, USA
abstract:
Holocene records of environmental changecapture the interrelated evolution of climate, ecosystems, and early humanactivity, especially as societies in the Central Mediterranean transitionedtoward increasingly settled agropastoral lifestyles during the Middle Holocene. Disentangling the relative influences of postglacial climate variability andanthropogenic landscape modification remains challenging, particularly in thisclimatically sensitive region. Continuous sedimentary records from bothterrestrial and marine archives were analyzed using multiple biogeochemical andclimate proxies to reconstruct these parameters and relationships in the Central Mediterranean.
This work integrates organic (lipid biomarker, compound-specific isotope) and carbonate clumped isotope analyses fromterrestrial (coastal Croatian lake) and marine (Aegean Sea) sediment cores toassess changes in vegetation dynamics, fire activity, human lifestyles, temperature, and hydroclimate across the Central Mediterranean. Together, theserecords capture coupled ecological, climatic, and human-driven changes acrossthe Holocene (11, 700 kyrs–present), a period for which regional paleoclimatedata remain sparse.
Terrestrial biomarker results (*{n}-alkanes, PAHs, fecal stanols, GDGTs) spanning the Middle Holocene indicate intensifyinghuman activity coincident with wetter regional conditions, the combination ofwhich led to a temporary, localized enhancement of microbial activity. Tocontextualize these results within the regional climate space, we appliedproxies for temperature (GDGTs, carbonate clumped isotopes) and hydrology (compound-specific hydrogen isotopes) to both our terrestrial and marinerecords. Results indicate a warming, drying trend throughout the Holocene, withthe Middle Holocene a ‘transitional’ period tentatively punctuated byalternating wet/dry cycles. Ongoing hydrogen isotope analyses will betterconstrain the role of changing hydroclimate conditions on landscape evolutionand human activity in the Central Mediterranean.
By pairing biogeochemical indicators ofclimate variability, ecosystem conditions, and early human activity, this study1) provides a pathway for tracing the spatiotemporal evolution of humanlifestyle modes during a period of transitional climate dynamics, and 2) highlights the sensitivity of Central Mediterranean landscapes to even modestclimatic perturbations and anthropogenic impacts, offering a long-termperspective essential for assessing future environmental change in this rapidlywarming, drying region.

name: Juliana Drozd
title: Lipid Carbon Isotope Patterns as Metabolicand Environmental Proxies
authors: Juliana Drozd^{1}, Katherine Freeman^{1}, Elliott Mueller^{2}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA\n^{2} Department of Geological Sciences, University of Colorado Boulder, Boulder, CO, USA
abstract: The chemical structures and stable isotopecompositions of lipids preserved in the rock record, known as biomarkers (molecular fossils), serve as proxies for properties that can be used toreconstruct past ecology and climates. Reconstructions based on biomarkerproxies rely on knowledge of how organisms, specifically primary producers, change their lipid production in response to growth conditions. Metabolicregulation triggered by environmental change is difficult to assess with thebiomarker record. However, differences in the carbon isotope compositionsbetween different types of lipids potentially capture signs of metabolicregulation because the flux of metabolites through branch points inbiosynthetic pathways can control the expression of isotope effects by enzymes. Fluxes are regulated in response to an organism’s needs and its environmentalconditions but are also subject to constraints from the organism’s physiology, including the compartmentalization of eukaryotic cells. We used metabolic reactionnetwork isotopologue modeling and comparison to existing datasets to assessthese signatures for green algae, haptophyte algae, cryptomonad algae, anddiatoms. In many algae, fatty acid biosynthesis is upregulated due toenvironmental stresses like temperature changes and nutrient starvation. Thisresults in a decreased difference in the carbon isotope compositions of fattyacids and phytol, an important isoprenoid lipid. For green algae, sterolbiosynthesis is co-regulated with fatty acid biosynthesis, which results insterols becoming ^{13}C-enriched relative to phytol when the algae areunder environmental stress. We can potentially use the differences in the δ^{13} Cvalues of different types of lipids as a proxy for environmental stress-inducedmetabolic regulation in eukaryotic algae. These findings for modern algalcultures might be able to be expanded to the biomarker record to spotpaleoenvironmental conditions that would have stressed ancient algalpopulations.

name: Em White
title: Reworking of Hadean crust: Evidence from µ^{142} Ndanomalies in later Archean crust
authors: Emily L. White^{1}, Michelle Jordan^{2}, Steven B. Shirey^{2}, Timothy Mock^{2}, D. Graham Pearson^{3}, William J. Davis^{3}, Jesse R. Reimink^{1}
institutions:
^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
^{2} Earth and Planets Laboratory, Carnegie Institution for Science, Washington, DC, USA
^{3} Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB, Canada
^{4} Natural Resources of Canada, Geological Survey of Canada, Ottawa, ON, Canada
abstract: Earth’s dynamic lithosphere sets it apart fromother observable silicate planetary bodies, as it features active andmobile-lid plate tectonics. However, the evolution/onset of these modern-styledplate tectonics, which have shaped Earth into the habitable world it is today, remains a fundamental and widely debated topic in the Earth sciences. The rateof net-continental growth throughout Earth history is required to evaluate theevolution of these geodynamical processes. One consequence of tectonics is howover billions of years of Earth history the continental crust is often altered, overprinted, and/or reworked. This has led to a paucity of ancient crustalmaterial preserved at the surface, limiting our record of Earth’s earliestcontinental crust and making it difficult to evaluate crustal growth throughtime. However, developments in high-precision whole-rock analysis of theshort-lived ^{146} Sm-^{142} Nd isotopic system allow us to traceanomalous signatures of ancient precursors in the products of later magmatism, enhancing this record.\nThe Slave Craton (Canadian Shield) hostsexcellent candidates for observing ancient crustal reworking, due to itsnear-constant record of episodic Archean crustal growth. It features 4020-2850Ma gneisses in the Central Slave Basement Complex (including the oldest knownzircon-bearing rock in its Acasta Gneiss Complex) and in the Tree River region. Additionally, 2650-2580 Ma granitoids occur across the province, with previousPb-isotope and long-lived Nd-isotope data indicating derivation from both ancientand juvenile sources. We present µ^{142} Nd (^{142} Nd/^{144} Ndnormalized to the bulk terrestrial composition) values of fourteen Neoarcheanand Meso- to Eo-Archean gneisses from across the Slave Craton. Our resultsdocument a more widespread presence of Hadean signatures in Eoarchean crustthan previously reported (ca. -16 ppm µ^{142} Nd), and some anomalous Neoarchean granitoids suggesting possible derivation from ancient crustalreworking. These results will test for widespread reworking of Hadeancontinental crust, improving our understanding crustal growth through time.

name: Rory Changleng
title: Disentangling Polygenetic Zircon Populations from Archaean Gneisses Reveals a New Eoarchaean Terrane
authors: Rory Changleng^{1}, Erik J. Schoonover^{1}, Cristy Stoian^{1, 2}, JoshuaM. Garber^{1, 3}, D. Graham Pearson^{4}, Yan Luo^{4, 5}, Jesse R. Reimink^{1}
institutions:
^{1} Department of Geosciences, Pennsylvania State University, PA, USA
^{2} Department of Geology, Colorado School of Mines, CO, USA
^{3} School of Earth and Environmental Sciences, University of St Andrews, St Andrews, UK
^{4} Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, University of Alberta, Edmonton, AB, Canada
^{5} Ken Williams Radiogenic Isotope Geoscience Laboratory, Texas A&M University, College Station, TX, USA
abstract:
A principal limitation of our understandingof the early Earth is the paucity of samples preserved from this time. Only around a dozen locations worldwide retain crust from the Eoarchaean(>3.6 Ga), and the true ages of many of these ancient vestiges of our planetremain hotly debated. One of the best recorders of crustal formation andalteration events is the mineral zircon. However, distinguishing betweenmultiple igneous and metamorphic events experienced by a zircon populationwithin an Archaean gneiss defines a critical question: how old is this rock?
Each tract of ancient crust discovered carriesa disproportionate significance in shedding light on the magmatic andgeodynamic conditions shaping our planet's earliest evolution. Consequently, careful evaluation is required when assessing whether a terrane preserves suchancient lithologies. We present a new U-Pb zircon geochronology from threebasement gneisses from the Eokuk Uplift, northwest Slave Craton. This regionrepresents an excellent target to search for new remnants of old crust due tosuperb outcrop exposure, proximity to the 4.03 Ga Acasta Gneiss Complex, andits relatively understudied nature resulting from its remote Arctic setting.
All three gneisses are complex andpolydeformed, with zircon age populations spanning more than 500 million years. We employ depth-profile analysis to target zircon rim domains and integratethese data with cathodoluminescence SEM imaging to aid in interpretingconventional LA–ICP–MS spot analyses. This combined approach allows us toreconstruct zircon crystallisation and alteration histories for each sample.
Although Eoarchaean-aged zircons occur in allthree gneisses, only one sample preserves a primary igneous zircon populationrecording the original crystallisation age of the host rock. At 3.81 Ga, thissample demonstrates that Eoarchaean crust is more widespread within the Slave Craton than previously recognised, significantly expanding the materialavailable for studying the earliest chapters of Earth’s history.

name: Fran Meyer
title: Oxidized uranium in organic-rich shalesfrom reducing environments
authors: Fran Meyer^{1}, Anthony Chappaz^{2}, Dan Gregory^{3}, Eve Carrothers^{3}, Erik Sperling^{4}, Justin Strauss^{5}, Lucien Nana Yobo^{6}, Kimberly Lau^{1}
institutions:
^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, PA, USA
^{2} Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences, Central Michigan University, Mount Pleasant, MI, USA
^{3} Department of Earth Sciences, University of Toronto, Toronto, ON, CA
^{4} Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, USA
^{5} Department of Earth Sciences, Dartmouth College, Hanover, NH, USA

abstract: The availability of oxygen in the Earth’sancient ocean and atmosphere is a key parameter for understanding Precambrianand Paleozoic biotic evolution and nutrient cycling. Due to the lack of directoxygen measurements in deep time, we must turn to the geochemical signaturespreserved in the sedimentary record. The enrichments and isotope ratios ofredox-sensitive elements deposited in marine basins, like U, provide a way toreconstruct changes in ocean oxygen availability. However, these proxies rely onmany unverified assumptions of how their solubility, speciation, and burial arecontrolled by redox conditions. Currently, interpreting U in reducing marineshales as a paleo-redox proxy assumes that burial and isotope fractionation areonly associated with the reduction of U (VI) to U (IV), and sequestration ofU (VI) and U (V) is negligible. Yet, the burial pathways and speciation of U inreducing marine environments still need to be defined. Without characterizingthe oxidation states or phase associations of U in marine shales, interpretations of the U-based proxies remain uncertain.\nIn this study, we use synchrotron-based X-rayfluorescence imaging and spatially resolved X-ray absorption near edgespectroscopy (XANES) at the U L3-edge paired with high energy resolutionfluorescence detection XANES at the U M4-edge to determine the spatialdistribution and speciation of U in marine shales from multiple localities andtime intervals. Samples included outcrop and drill core shales from the Cretaceous Eagle Ford Group, the Devonian Marcellus Formation, and the Ordovician Road River Group. XANES spectra at both the U L3- and M4-edgesuggest that three U oxidation states (IV, V and VI) are present, despite proxydata suggesting anoxic depositional settings. The ubiquitous presence of U (V) and U (VI) in marine shales from reducing environments adds new understanding ofthe U marine cycle and challenges the current use of U as a paleo-redox proxy.

name: Hanna Leapaldt
title: Signatures of microbial carbon cyclingin magnesium carbonate minerals
authors: Hanna C. Leapaldt^{1}, Tori C. Cassady^{2}, Frank A. Corsetti^{2}, Miquela Ingalls^{1}
institutions: ^{1} Department of Geosciences, The Pennsylvania State University, Pennsylvania, 16802, USA\n^{2} Department of Earth Sciences, University of Southern California, California, 90089, USA
abstract: Magnesium carbonate minerals have beenidentified in the Jezero Crater paleolake basin on Mars and have been collectedby *{Perseverance} to be evaluated for potential biosignatures. However, there is not yet a diagnostic set of textural, geochemical, and isotopiccharacteristics that can distinguish biotic from abiotic magnesium carbonateminerals. We compared magnesium carbonate samples that form biotically – frommicrobial mats and shallow sediments in two hyperalkaline lake/playa systems in British Columbia (South Atlin Playa and Alberta Lake) – to those formingabiotically from carbonation of serpentinite in bedrock. We used a novelisotope system (dual-clumped isotopes; Δ_{47}-Δ_{48}) andhypothesized that biological carbon cycling within the microbial mats willcause kinetic isotope effects resulting in Δ_{47}-Δ_{48}disequilibrium signatures. We measured the Δ_{47}and Δ_{48}values every 5 cm of 15 cm cores through the microbial mats as well as from thesubsampled bedrock. All microbial mat cores revealed the same, distinctivetrend with depth: the Δ_{47}-Δ_{48} values of samples in theupper 5 cm of the cores within microbial mat, where we expect activecyanobacterial photosynthesis, yielded the largest offset from the Δ_{47}-Δ_{48}theoretical equilibrium. The microbial mat sample Δ_{47}-Δ_{48}values yield disequilibrium signatures expected for association withphotoautotrophy. We interpret the observed values to be a signature ofcyanobacterial photosynthesis at the mat surface causing CO2 degassing, leadingto the observed -Δ_{47}/+Δ_{48} kineticisotope effects. Fluorescently labelled embedded core images from the upper 5cm at both locations reveal cellular material incorporated into the fabric ofthe sediment, providing evidence of a microbial control on carbon cycling. Ifsuch kinetic isotope effects are absent from abiotically formed magnesiumcarbonate minerals, dual-clumped isotopes can provide a tool to help identifybiogenicity of magnesium carbonate minerals when paired with other evidencelike textural analysis.

title: From aquatic ferns to rainforest trees: Thefirst plant macrofossils from the early Eocene Ghazij Formation record adiverse flora and associated insect herbivory on the Indian Subcontinent
authors: Edward J. Spagnuolo^{1}, Peter Wilf^{1}, P. J. Przybylski^{1}, L. Alejandro Giraldo^{1}, Munir ul-Haq^{2}, Scott L. Wing^{3}, William C. Clyde^{4}

abstract: Well-dated plant fossils from tropical Asiaare rare, limiting understanding of how and when this region attained itsfloral composition and high species richness. Here, we report the first plantmacrofossils and associated insect damage from the early Eocene Ghazij Formation (Balochistan, Pakistan), well known for its mammalian faunas thatdocument early biotic interchange associated with the India (Indo-Pakistan)-Asia collision. The macrofossils were collected from 15 sitesfrom the middle and upper Ghazij, totaling 420 compression specimens, primarilyof leaves, dating to the early Eocene Climatic Optimum (EECO). The flora has anestimated 40 species, dominated by Sapindaceae (maple, lychee family) leafletsaffiliated to the rainforest tree *{Pometia}, and multiple Fabaceae (legumefamily) and Arecaceae (palm) morphotypes. The *{Pometia-}like leaflets arethe oldest macrofossils potentially affiliated to the genus and would supportits proposed Indian biogeographic history based on prior pollen data. Rarermorphotypes include Menispermaceae (moonseeds), possible Rhamnaceae (buckthorns), possible *{Calophyllum, }Araceae (*{Monstera} family), *{}and the aquatic ferns *{Acrostichum }and*{ Salvinia}.Insect-feeding damage is diverse and abundant, totaling 47 damage types (DTs), including nine hole feeding DTs, seven piercing and sucking DTs, 13 gall DTs, and six mines. Adjusted for sample size, the Ghazij flora has some of thehighest herbivory levels in the fossil record (although mining is rare), providing novel information about tropical plant-animal interactions during theEECO.

name: Dani Buchheister
title: The iron-sulfur world in a bottle: FeS_{2}formation in microbial enrichment cultures
authors: Dani Buchheister^{1}, Kenneth Broad^{2}, Nadir Quarta^{3}, Julie Cosmidis^{4}, Jennifer Macalady^{1}
institutions:

abstract: The Frasassi cave system in central Italyhosts a permanently stratified sulfidic aquifer with a shallow microoxic zoneand a deeper anoxic zone. The deep aquifer lacks most of the oxidants used forrespiration by surface life, and has sulfate concentrations of approximatelyone-eighth of marine, making it a promising analog for Proterozoic oceans. Biofilms in the deep aquifer contain abundant pyrite (FeS, ) mineral grains anda treasure trove of microbial “dark matter, ” microorganisms with only distant relativesin public databases. There are multiple formation pathways for FeS2, and therole that microbes play in iron sulfide mineral nucleation and crystal growthis the topic of ongoing debate.\nIn February 2023, Frasassi deep aquiferbiofilms were retrieved to inoculate enrichment cultures targeting a “missing”metabolism–Wächtershäuser’s proposed pyrite- and hydrogen-producing metabolismthat reacts iron sulfide (FeS) with hydrogen sulfide. After a year ofincubation, clusters of cells and microspheroidal mineral grains were observedwith transmitted light and epifluorescence microscopy. Further imaging andmineral analyses were performed using Raman spectroscopy and SEM-EDS. DNAextracted from the biofilm (inoculum) and the enrichment cultures were analyzedusing 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing to determine the taxonomy of the majorpopulations. Metagenomic sequences were also obtained for the enrichmentculture. Raman and SEM-EDS data indicate the presence of FeS_{2} in theenrichment culture bottles but not in the abiotic controls. FeS_{2}mineral grains are microspheroidal but do not look like microbially-mediatedpyrite produced in other laboratory studies. The enrichment communities showchanges in taxonomic structure from the native biofilm and are much lessdiverse. Known sulfur cyclers are abundant in the bottles, yielding clues tothe potential role of the enrichment microbes in FeS_{2} formation.
